kp.k: Four scenarios frame possible AI-era business models
kp.d: The authors present four distinct strategic paths for legal-service delivery over the next decade: tech-led disruptor, elite boutique, integrated powerhouse, and traditional regulated firm. They explicitly characterize these as scenarios rather than predictions, although they assert that elements of all four already exist and anticipate that their relative market dominance will change by 2030.
qs: To help law firm leaders navigate these strategic choices, the Thomson Reuters Institute has developed four potential business model scenarios for how legal services might be delivered and purchased over the next decade.

These scenarios are not predictions; rather, they represent distinct strategic paths that firms could pursue, each with different implications for talent, pricing, client relationships, and competitive positioning.
Seeds of all four of these scenarios already exist today. What will change by 2030 is which scenarios will dominate, not whether they're each possible.

kp.k: Strategic ambiguity creates a dangerous competitive middle
kp.d: The central argument is that firms must select and communicate a differentiated business model. Firms that are neither highly automated, genuinely elite, globally scaled, nor protected by regulation constitute the “dangerous middle”; current profitability and competent work are said to be insufficient without a compelling future value proposition.
qs: The dangerous middle ground comprises law firms without clear strategic positioning — neither fully automated, nor elite premium, nor true global scale, nor protected by regulation.
Even though they’re doing good work for reasonable clients at fair rates, that’s no longer enough.
The bottom line is that strategic clarity beats strategic ambiguity. Firms that attempt to be “a bit of everything” risk being squeezed from all sides.

kp.k: Clients already assess outside counsel’s AI maturity
kp.d: The source asserts that, by the middle of 2025, corporate legal departments were using outside firms’ AI capabilities as a selection criterion, sometimes before developing their own AI strategies. Its supporting examples are qualitative: comments from a multibillion-dollar retailer’s legal leader and the practices of one large technology company, rather than a quantified market study.
qs: By the middle of 2025, many corporate legal departments began evaluating their outside law firms based on AI capabilities — even while figuring out their own strategies.

The legal department leader of a multibillion-dollar retail company spoke with the Thomson Reuters Institute about their approach to AI and legal spend. They said they’re still working out the basics, but they've made one expectation clear to their outside firms: articulate how AI will deliver better quality and greater efficiency, now.

One large technology company's legal department co-designs AI workflows with outside counsel, mandating specific tool use at specific workflow stages and benchmarking quality outcomes against best-attorney baselines.

kp.k: Automatable work creates existential pressure for firms
kp.d: The authors argue that firms whose portfolios contain more than half automatable work need fundamentally different strategies. They expect repeatable and routine work to migrate either to technology platforms or into corporate legal departments, potentially leaving smaller firms unable to absorb regulatory compliance costs or compete with larger providers on price.
qs: For example, if more than half of a firm's work is susceptible to automation, that firm needs a fundamentally different strategy.
As AI offers efficiency gains around repeatable, routine tasks, corporate legal departments will migrate this work to tech platforms or automate it in-house.
Firms that can automate more than half of their legal work will face existential pressure.

kp.k: Tech-led disruptors automate high-volume legal work
kp.d: The first scenario envisages AI-native, subscription-based platforms providing nearly self-service legal services, with lawyers supervising systems and intervening mainly in edge cases. The authors identify standardized contracts, entity formation, compliance filings, trademark applications, and plaintiff-side workflow stages as suitable where parameters are well defined, variables are limited, and strategic judgment is unnecessary.
qs: In our first scenario, AI-native platforms would deliver legal services with minimal human oversight through self-service subscription models.
Nearly all work would be fully automated, with humans intervening only for edge cases.
The pattern is consistent — you need well-defined legal parameters, limited variables, and outcomes that don't require strategic judgment.

kp.k: Automation could reduce costs and expand service access
kp.d: Proponents of the tech-led model predict cost reductions potentially reaching 80%. If achieved at scale, the authors argue that this model could give small and midsize businesses access to sophisticated services previously available mainly to large corporations; this is a conditional forecast, not a reported measured outcome.
qs: Proponents argue this model could achieve dramatic cost reductions — potentially up to 80% — by automating compliance, drafting, and research work.
If this model emerges at scale, small and midsize businesses would gain access to sophisticated legal services that were previously available only to large corporations.
A small number of attorneys supervise these AI platforms, managing case volumes that once required substantial staffing, enabling the dramatic cost reductions this model promises.

kp.k: AI-native providers may outperform traditional delivery structures
kp.d: For the highly automated scenario, the source identifies technology companies and ALSPs developing use-case-specific AI as best positioned. Plaintiff-side firms may also benefit because high case volumes and contingency fees create incentives to automate intake, document preparation, and settlement negotiations.
qs: Plaintiff-side firms may be particularly well positioned for this model because the volume economics and contingency-fee structures create strong incentives to automate case intake, document preparation, and settlement negotiations.
Technology companies and alternative legal service providers building use-case-specific AI are best positioned for this approach.

kp.k: Elite boutiques combine premium judgment with AI augmentation
kp.d: The second scenario is an augmentation model for unusually complex and consequential matters. A limited number of firms would charge rates 50% to 100% above average, using AI and technology specialists to support senior partners while preserving human judgment, creativity, negotiation, and relationship management as the core sources of value.
qs: In this scenario, a select number of firms would command premium rates 50% to 100% above average for the highest-stakes, most complex work.
Senior partners would receive support from technology specialists rather than teams of associates.
The work would require uniquely human capabilities — judgment, creativity, and complex negotiation skills — with minimal routine work remaining.

kp.k: Elite teams replace associate pyramids with specialists
kp.d: The elite-boutique scenario predicts a sharp reduction in traditional leverage: teams of 20 or more associates would be replaced by two to three senior partners and technology specialists. Partner roles would shift toward business-risk advice, strategic counseling, deal facilitation, and policy strategy rather than routine processing.
qs: Client teams would transform dramatically — replacing the traditional pyramid of 20 or more associates with two to three senior partners plus technology specialists.

For example, mergers and acquisitions (M&A) partners would become business risk advisors and deal facilitators, litigation partners would become strategic counselors that can navigate high-stakes disputes, and regulatory partners would be policy strategists rather than compliance processors.

kp.k: True premium positioning can support few firms
kp.d: The authors qualify the elite-boutique path by arguing that market economics can sustain only a limited number of genuinely premium firms. Large full-service firms in the broad middle cannot obtain this position merely through generally good lawyers or quality work; they would require proprietary expertise in discrete, high-stakes fields.
qs: However, market economics can support only a limited number of firms in a true premium position such as this.
In this case, “boutique” means selective — this path cannot support firms currently in the broad middle, including many large, full-service law firms.
Firms in this category would need to have genuinely proprietary expertise in discrete, high-stakes practice areas, not merely good lawyers doing quality work.

kp.k: Integrated powerhouses systematize sophisticated repeatable work
kp.d: The third scenario combines global scale, complete automation of commodity work, and standardized AI-enabled workflows for sophisticated but repeatable matters. Unlike elite boutiques handling unprecedented work, these firms would maintain premium positioning by delivering consistent quality across jurisdictions and practice areas through process excellence.
qs: In this third scenario, large global law firms would leverage their scale advantages through systematized approaches and AI-enabled delivery teams — the legal industry's equivalent of elite consulting firms that deliver top-tier quality through process excellence, not despite it.
The critical transformation is that commodity work would be automated entirely, allowing firms to systematize sophisticated but repeatable tasks to elite-quality standards.
Unprecedented and novel matters would go to the elite boutiques; however, sophisticated but repeatable work — whether single- or multijurisdictional — would flow to these integrated powerhouses.

kp.k: Global scale requires substantial infrastructure investment
kp.d: The integrated-powerhouse model is associated with cross-border and cross-practice orchestration, senior-partner strategic direction, and technology-enabled execution. The source suggests that firms operating in 50 or more countries possess the necessary scale, while warning that success requires major investment in process infrastructure, knowledge management, and standardized delivery methods.
qs: Client teams for these powerhouses would involve cross-border, cross-practice orchestration in which senior partners provide strategic direction while technology-enabled teams execute systematized workflows globally.
Global platform firms with a presence spanning 50 or more countries excel in this model because they have the necessary scale and can meet the significant consolidation required to succeed.
On this path, success demands heavy investment in process infrastructure, knowledge management systems, and standardized delivery methodologies.

kp.k: Regulation may temporarily preserve traditional human delivery
kp.d: The fourth scenario assumes licensing and bar requirements continue to require lawyer oversight or sign-off, restricting fully automated delivery for court filings, regulatory submissions, and certified legal work. The authors assert that California and New York already mandate lawyer involvement in AI-assisted work, but characterize regulatory protection as temporary because competitive and client pressure may eventually erode barriers.
qs: In this scenario, bar association rules and professional licensing requirements would mandate human lawyer oversight for many legal services, limiting AI deployment despite its groundbreaking technological capabilities.

Major jurisdictions within the United States, including California and New York, already mandate lawyer involvement in AI-assisted work, with bar associations actively resisting changes that would allow greater automation.
However, this protection would be a delay, not an immunity.

kp.k: AI adoption alone does not constitute transformation
kp.d: The authors distinguish purchasing AI tools from redesigning workflows and value propositions. They argue that firms focused only on early-stage adoption risk falling behind competitors already pursuing “Wave 3” business-model transformation, and predict that strategic redesign rather than deployment speed will determine which firms thrive.
qs: In fact, the firms that do thrive won't be those deploying AI tools fastest — they'll be those redesigning their businesses around fundamentally different value propositions.
Your AI strategy consists of buying tools without changing how work gets done
Indeed, while too many firms are still focused on the Wave 1 adoption — outlined in the white paper mentioned previously — their future competitors are already building Wave 3 business models.

kp.k: Leaders should audit work and choose direction
kp.d: The recommended response is to classify revenue by routine, sophisticated, and unprecedented work; assess the share that is fully automatable; survey clients about AI expectations; test partnership alignment; select a scenario; identify capability, talent, and technology gaps; and pilot the model in one practice area rather than continuing indefinite planning.
qs: First, audit the volume and nature of your work matters. Categorize revenue by complexity level — routine, sophisticated, or unprecedented — to understand your exposure.
Survey your clients explicitly about their AI expectations rather than assuming you know what they want.
Start a pilot program in a single practice area to learn by doing rather than planning indefinitely.

kp.k: AI may drive consolidation and fewer firms
kp.d: Looking toward 2030, the source predicts that lawyers, client relationships, and professional judgment will remain, but the overall market will be transformed by consolidation, fewer firms, a different distribution of firm sizes, and new dominant providers. This is a forward-looking scenario claim rather than an empirically demonstrated finding.
qs: The close-up view of 2030 will still show lawyers, firms, client relationships, and professional judgment.
However, if you take a step back, the market composition becomes unrecognizable due to significant consolidation, fewer firms, dramatically different size distribution, and new dominant players.
Indeed, the firms that will dominate by 2030 are making their strategic choices now, while competitors debate which tools to buy.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Elizabeth Duffy and Ragunath Ramanathan describe four conditional AI-era business models, alongside claims that client selection criteria, work allocation, staffing and market structure are already changing or will change.
pts.d: The authors explicitly present the four scenarios as strategic possibilities rather than predictions. (1) Tech-led disruptor: AI-native platforms could provide routine legal services through self-service subscriptions with minimal human oversight. They attribute potential cost reductions of up to 80% to proponents of this model. Compliance, drafting and research would be automated, with attorneys handling exceptions and supervising volumes previously requiring substantial staffing. Plaintiff-side firms could automate intake, document preparation and settlement negotiations; small and midsize businesses could gain access to services previously available only to large corporations. (2) Elite boutique: a limited number of firms could charge 50%–100% above average for exceptionally complex, high-stakes work, using AI to augment rather than replace premium expertise. Teams of 20 or more associates would give way to two or three senior partners supported by technology specialists. M&A, litigation and regulatory partners would become business risk advisors, strategic counselors and policy strategists rather than routine processors. (3) Integrated powerhouse: large global firms could automate commodity work and systematize sophisticated, repeatable work, maintaining premium positioning through consistent delivery across comprehensive client needs. Senior partners would direct technology-enabled execution teams; scale, consolidation and investment in process infrastructure would underpin the model. (4) Traditional firm: professional rules could preserve human delivery and sign-off, limiting AI to a supporting role and imposing compliance costs on clients. The authors expect this protection eventually to weaken under competition and client pressure. Beyond the scenarios, they claim corporate buyers already assess outside firms' AI capabilities, predict migration of repeatable work to platforms or in-house automation, and warn of existential pressure on firms with more than half their work automatable. They forecast a consolidated market with fewer firms and new dominant players by 2030. Firms lacking differentiation, automation, premium expertise, scale or regulatory protection constitute a vulnerable 'dangerous middle'; business redesign and clear positioning, rather than tool acquisition alone, are presented as the basis of future success.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source offers a prior strategic framework, two anonymized corporate-client examples and regulatory assertions; it provides no measured results or methods supporting its numerical scenario estimates or market forecasts.
pts.d: The authors build on the three-wave framework in Thomson Reuters' February 2025 'The future of the law firm' white paper, using Wave 3 business-model redesign as their conceptual basis. For current buyer behavior, they report a conversation with the legal department leader of an unnamed multibillion-dollar retail company. That leader reportedly requires outside firms to explain immediate quality and efficiency benefits from AI despite the department not yet having its own integration strategy, because counsel selection covers the next three years. The source also describes an unnamed large technology company's legal department co-designing AI workflows, prescribing tool use and benchmarking quality against best-attorney baselines. It gives no benchmark results, methodology or identified company. The authors generalize these examples into a broader pattern of buyer demand exceeding buyer AI maturity, but supply no survey size, adoption percentages or systematic dataset. Their regulatory scenario cites California and New York and professional licensing requirements as sources of mandatory lawyer involvement, without identifying specific rules or legal authorities. The 80% potential cost reduction is attributed to unspecified proponents; the 50%–100% premium, proposed staffing configurations, more-than-half automation threshold and 2030 consolidation outlook are presented without supporting calculations or empirical estimates. The claimed advantages of each scenario are explained through task characteristics, economics and organizational requirements rather than demonstrated performance.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source locates client pressure in mid-2025 and the present, frames scenarios over the next decade, and identifies 2030 as a market-transformation horizon; each model depends on distinct task, capability or regulatory conditions.
pts.d: Writing in 2026, Duffy and Ramanathan say many corporate departments began evaluating outside firms' AI capabilities by the middle of 2025. Current choices are said to determine which firms dominate by 2030, while the four scenarios concern potential delivery and purchasing models over the next decade. The retail-client example concerns counsel selection for the next three years. Tech-led disruption depends on well-defined legal parameters, limited variables and outcomes not requiring strategic judgment; broader service access is conditional on the model emerging at scale. The elite boutique requires genuinely proprietary expertise in discrete, high-stakes areas and is explicitly constrained by limited demand for true premium providers. Integrated powerhouses require the ability to systematize sophisticated repeatable work, substantial infrastructure and knowledge-management investment, and coordination across practices and, where necessary, borders; the source identifies global platforms spanning 50 or more countries as especially suited. Traditional firms retain protection only where jurisdiction or matter type requires human involvement. The authors call such protection temporary and predict erosion under competitive and client pressure, without specifying when rules will change. The survival warnings are conditional on automation exposure and weak positioning, rather than predictions that all firms or all legal work will be displaced.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The proposed changes redistribute routine, sophisticated-repeatable and unprecedented work among platforms, in-house departments, global firms and elite boutiques, while reducing associate-heavy delivery and exposing undifferentiated firms.
pts.d: Corporate legal departments are buyers evaluating outside counsel, potentially internalizing routine work and specifying AI-enabled workflows. Small and midsize businesses could receive more sophisticated services through lower-cost platforms; this is a business-service access claim, not an explicit claim about closing the civil justice gap. Technology companies and ALSPs building use-case-specific AI are identified as well positioned for tech-led delivery, with plaintiff-side firms benefiting from volume and contingency-fee incentives. Routine-service segments include NDAs, standard employment contracts, basic entity formation, compliance filings and straightforward trademark applications. Elite boutiques would handle bet-the-company M&A, novel regulation, complex cross-border disputes and high-stakes IP litigation; many large full-service firms in the broad middle would not qualify merely by employing good lawyers. Associates would be displaced from the boutique's proposed team structure, while senior partners and technology specialists gain central roles. Integrated global firms would deliver standardized diligence, multijurisdictional regulatory reviews, global employment work and large contract-management programs through coordinated technology-enabled teams. Traditional firms handling filings, submissions and attorney-certified work could retain protected positions, while clients bear human-sign-off costs. Smaller firms could lose profitability or clients because of compliance overhead and larger competitors' lower prices. Firms of any size without a clear position face the greatest squeeze.
